Learning Objectives
Understand the etiology and definition of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita.
Recognize the most common types of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita.
Identify the workup for the most common diagnoses associated with arthrogryposis multiplex
congenita.
Understand the natural history of arthrogryposis.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (AMC), or simply arthrogryposis, is a term for a
heterogeneous group of conditions resulting in a baby born with multiple congenital
contractures.

More than 400 separate conditions have been identified as causative; commonality between
these conditions is a lack of intrauterine movement (fetal akinesia).
Most underlying conditions are rare. The more common conditions are Amyoplasia, some
distal arthrogryposes, and Escobar syndrome.

Overview
AMC is not a diagnosis but a descriptive term for the phenotype of a child born with
contractures of two or more different body areas.1-3 For example, a child born with
bilateral clubfoot deformities alone does not have arthrogryposis; however, a child born
with a clubfoot and a knee flexion contracture fits the definition of arthrogryposis. More
than 400 known gene mutations can lead to a child with AMC;4 however, a number of
nongenetic conditions (eg, Amyoplasia, maternal Zika infection, intrauterine crowding)
also can lead to a child with AMC. The commonality between these conditions is that the
fetus experiences a lack of movement of the limbs involved, to the extreme in severe
cases of an essentially immobile fetus during pregnancy. Amyoplasia (capitalized) refers
specifically to the nongenetic classical arthrogryposis,5 the most common form of AMC,
whereas amyoplasia (not capitalized) nonspecifically indicates a congenital generalized
lack of muscular development and growth. Orthopaedic management involves
improving positioning of joints and improving joint range of motion.
Epidemiology
The estimated incidence of AMC is 1:3,000 to 1:5,000 live births.6
Amyoplasia (classic arthrogryposis) accounts for one-third of live cases (1:10,000)
Distal arthrogryposes account for approximately one-fifth of live cases.7

Epidemiology
The underlying finding is lack of intrauterine motion; therefore, the contractures occur in
the fetal period and are deformations, rather than malformations that would have

Patients with amyoplasia may present with varying levels of involvement9 (Figure 1).
All-four-limb involvement: 46% to 84%
Lower-limb involvement only: 11% to 43%
Upper-limb involvement only: 5% to 11%
Scoliosis in approximately 30%.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
No congenital bone malformations other than the small subgroup of skeletal dysplasias with
congenital contractures
Babies may be born with disuse osteopenia, making them susceptible to fractures of long
bones during the birthing process, most commonly the humerus and femur.
Vascular
Major vascular architecture usually is preserved.
In some pterygium (joint webbing) syndromes, the neurovascular bundle may be displaced
into the pterygium, particularly anterior to the elbow and posterior to the knee (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Conventional arteriogram of the left lower extremity of 1-month-old boy shows bridging
of vascular structures within a popliteal pterygium. Arrowheads indicate the posteriorly displaced

(Reproduced with permission from Donnelly LF, Emery KH, Do TT: MR imaging of popliteal
pterygium syndrome in pediatric patients. AJR Am J Roentgenol 2002;178[5]:1281-1284.)
Nerves
Depending on the underlying condition, the peripheral nerves may be variably involved.
Hypoplasia of select anterior horn cells (AHCs) may lead to diminution of functioning lower
motor neurons associated with affected muscles, as observed in Amyoplasia.
Tendons
In most of the conditions, the muscle-tendon architecture is preserved.
In the pterygium conditions, the tendinous fascia often become confluent, such as the
hamstrings fascia flowing into the gastrocnemius fascia.
Joints and Ligaments
Depending on the severity of joint involvement and age of the patient:
Articular surfaces may be flattened or deformed
Variable arthrofibrosis
Stiff and contracted ligaments
Musculature
Overall architecture of the muscle groups is preserved.
The quality of the muscle may vary considerably, from normal-appearing muscle tissue to
complete replacement by adipose tissue.
Subcutaneous Adipose Tissue
Relatively stiff and inelastic, somewhat woody, and may decrease skin mobility
May lead to postoperative skin-healing problems.

The lack of spontaneous motion inhibits the normal development of joints, potentially
affecting every tissue layer. The skin over a joint is less elastic, often lacking creases,
such as the ones normally appearing on the dorsum of hand digits. The skin may be
tethered to underlying structures, creating dimples, often observed at the posterior
elbow, over the greater trochanter, or over the patella. The subcutaneous fat also is less
elastic, with a firm or “woody” consistency, further limiting skin mobility. The lack of
adipose remodeling around joints may indicate a thicker subcutaneous layer, such as
posterior to the knee. Tendons do not undergo normal gliding in their sheaths during
development, causing limited excursion or possibly complete fibrosis. Ligaments are stiff
and contracted, which, in combination with a contracted or adhered joint capsule,
intrinsically limits joint motion. The shape of the articular surface is initially normal;
however, over time, the lack of motion brings about congruent flattening of opposing
joint surfaces. In severe cases, arthrofibrosis will occur during childhood, more severely
threatening the ability to gain motion.
In most forms of arthrogryposis, the muscles are the final common pathway for fetal
akinesia. Whether the etiology is primarily muscular (distal arthrogryposes, congenital
muscular dystrophies or myopathies) or neurologic, functioning muscle usually is
pink/red and healthy, but nonfunctioning muscle will undergo disuse atrophy and
complete adipose replacement. On direct visualization, the fat-replaced muscle will
appear striated and be compartmentalized but will be non-contractile.
An occasional characteristic of AMC is a spiral groove of the extremities, usually
observed in the thigh and/or lower leg. This represents wrapping of the umbilical cord
around the extremity, rather than an amniotic band9 (Figure 4). Release of this groove is
not indicated, except in the rare instances of signs of vascular compromise in the
extremity.

Etiology
Four hundred different underlying conditions can lead to a baby born with AMC.4
Fetal akinesia (lack of intrauterine motion during pregnancy) is the underlying commonality.
A few common causal pathways can lead to fetal akinesia.
The neurologic pathway may include structural or functional abnormalities of the brain;
spinal cord/upper motor neurons; hypoplasia of the AHCs; dysfunction of the neuromuscular
junction; or, rarely, peripheral nervous system defects.
The muscular pathway comprises a spectrum of congenital muscle conditions. The
congenital myopathies can be caused by mutations of genes fundamental to muscle
structure, as in many of the distal arthrogryposes. The hallmark of congenital myotonic
dystrophy is the inability to relax muscles at will. Some of the congenital muscular
dystrophies that cause arthrogryposis may be progressive after birth, leading to increasing

severity of joint contractures, which contrasts with nearly all other forms of arthrogryposis
that are nonprogressive.
Connective-tissue or soft-tissue abnormalities make up another diverse pathway. Some
skeletal dysplasias of the osteochondrodysplasic type involve arthrogrypotic contractures,
including Kniest syndrome, diastrophic dysplasia, and metatropic dysplasia. Collagen
disorders may result in muscle tissue replacement by connective tissue or thickening of joint
capsules, such as multiple pterygium syndrome (MPS) or Larsen syndrome.
Pregnancy environment pathway (intrauterine crowding, maternal illness, medications or
drugs) 
Natural History
Signs or symptoms of decreased movement may be apparent during pregnancy.
Birth often is via Caesarian section because of breech positioning.
Severely involved babies may be stillborn or die early.
Most children with AMC are cognitively intact and display adaptive skills in response to the
movement limitations.
Of those who survive the neonatal period, those with most forms of arthrogryposis will
experience a normal lifespan.

Natural History
The rate of neonatal diagnosis remains low. Despite mothers (usually those who have
experienced previous pregnancies) remarking on decreased fetal movement, current
ultrasonography protocols only diagnose approximately 25% of cases before 24 weeks
gestation.10,11 Studies have shown that nearly one-half of cases could be detected by 12
or 13 weeks via proper ultrasonography protocols.12 Early prenatal ultrasonography may
note decreased fetal movement, hand or foot deformities, and knees or elbows held in
extension. Ultrasonography also may detect fetal hydrops, cystic hygroma, or nuchal
edema. Lack of intrauterine breathing and swallowing may later lead to detection of
pulmonary hypoplasia, polyhydramnios, and absent stomach filling. Because of breech
positioning, many babies are delivered via Caesarian section. Fractures at birth may
occur because of positioning and intrauterine disuse osteopenia but should increase
suspicion for Bruck syndrome (arthrogryposis and osteogenesis imperfecta). SEND FEEDBACK

Lethal forms of arthrogryposis are very common. A study of 183 arthrogrypotic
pregnancies found that 3 babies were spontaneously lost before 20 gestational weeks,
18 babies were stillborn, and 50 babies died in their first year of life (most in the first
month). Including the 12 voluntary terminations of pregnancy, the total mortality rate
was 45%.8 Fetal akinesia deformation sequence (also known as Pena-Shokeir type 1) is a
severe form of AMC with intrauterine growth retardation, facial anomalies, and
pulmonary hypoplasia; 30% are stillborn, and many die early because of pulmonary
hypoplasia.13
Some patients with arthrogryposis may have mild to severe cognitive impairment, which
often is matched by their physical disabilities; however, most surviving children with
AMC will be cognitively intact. For those without cognitive or severe pulmonary
involvement, life expectancy is good.
Outcome studies show that people with AMC learn to adapt to their deformities as best
possible, such as learning to write using two hands to hold a pencil or using their nose or
tongue on a touch-screen digital device. Most adults with AMC are ambulatory (49% to
-88%); however, many use a wheelchair in the community or for longer distances, and
many drive automobiles (48% to 86%). Only 32% to 50% of survey respondents self-
describe as fully independent in their daily living, primarily because of upper extremity
functional limitations. Most patients with AMC (95% to 98%) have undergone
orthopaedic surgery, mostly during childhood. The mean number of procedures is 7 to
10 but may be as high as 45 procedures.14-18
Pain is a common complaint of adults with AMC, with 75% to 91% describing pain that
often is activity-limiting, particularly related to the lumbar spine and lower extremities
and occasionally the jaw and the upper extremities.14-17,19,20
Risk Factors
Identical twin births, especially if sharing the same placenta.
Familial genetic load
Maternal factors


Risk Factors
Causative factors for AMC appear to be relatively balanced between intrinsic (genetic)
and extrinsic risks.
Intrinsic risks are genetic conditions that can be passed down from one or both parents.
This is a sizable category with more than 400 different gene mutations associated with
AMC.4 Autosomal-dominant conditions include distal arthrogryposes (except DA5, which
is autosomal recessive); however, approximately one-half of new cases are de novo
mutations.21 Autosomal-recessive conditions include Escobar syndrome, titinopathy,
and arthrogryposis renal dysfunction cholestasis. An example of inherited X-linked gene
mutations is ZC4H2-associated rare disorders (ZARD), also known as Wieacker-Wolff
syndrome.
Placental sharing in monochorionic (identical) twin pregnancies is one of the more
common extrinsic risks. Whether the cause is true twin-twin transfusions or simply
insufficient vascular flow to the future arthrogrypotic fetus is unclear.9 Other extrinsic
factors include maternal illness (myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis) or infection
(rubella, rubeola, Zika, cytomegalovirus), intrauterine crowding (septate or bicornuate
uterus, uterine fibroids), and medication/drugs (methocarbamol, phenytoin, fetal alcohol
syndrome).
Classification
Given the wide heterogeneity of AMC, the creation of classification systems has been difficult.
Three common strategies are available for the classification of AMC.
Clinical involvement: separate conditions by body areas involved
Etiology of fetal akinesia: separate by the different pathways that result in a lack of
intrauterine motion
Cardinal features: group conditions by common characteristics

Classification
The functions of a classification system are to aid in diagnosis, enhance communication
between stakeholders, guide management, and help prognosticate. The extremely wide
range of underlying conditions that may lead to a child born with multiple contractures
presents a challenge in organizing the heterogeneity into a comprehensive classification
system. Two of the more commonly used strategies are2:
Clinical involvement
Group 1: primarily limb involvement (Amyoplasia, distal arthrogryposis type 1 [DA1],
Bruck syndrome)
Group 2: musculoskeletal involvement plus other system anomalies (Freeman-
Sheldon [DA2A] and Sheldon-Hall [DA2B] syndromes, DA3, DA4, DA5, DA6, DA7;
pterygium syndromes [Escobar, popliteal pterygium syndrome], Mobius syndrome)
Group 3: musculoskeletal involvement with associated central nervous system
dysfunction/malformation, with or without cognitive disability, including the lethal
arthrogryposes
Cardinal features
Amyoplasia: the most common single cause of AMC, nongenetic
Distal arthrogryposes: a group of conditions that are autosomal dominant with
variable expressivity (except DA5, which is autosomal recessive); many patients
present with de novo mutations; as a group, distal arthrogryposes represent the
second most common cause of AMC. Table 1 lists the most common distal
arthrogryposes.
Everything else, including the pterygium syndromes, X-linked conditions, teratogenic
syndromes, maternal illnesses, intellectual disability, fetal akinesia deforming
syndrome, and lethal conditions

Evaluation/Diagnosis—Amyoplasia

Evaluation/Diagnosis—Amyoplasia
Amyoplasia is the classic form of arthrogryposis. Occasionally, it is mistaken as the true
form of arthrogryposis, and by extension all other forms are not actually arthrogryposis.
This misunderstanding must be corrected because it can be very confusing to families
and complicate treatment decisions.
Patient History
The condition may be recognized in utero via ultrasonographic evaluation.
Babies may require the neonatal intensive care unit for feeding or breathing issues, but most
are healthy at birth.

Patient History

Prenatal history may include recognition of fetal akinesia, either by the mother who
noted decreased fetal movement or by unchanged fetal position from one
ultrasonographic evaluation to the next. Ultrasonography may identify limb deformities
(clubfoot and hand deformities most commonly) and findings of oligohydramnios and
intrauterine growth retardation. The presence of fetal cervical hyperextension should be
assessed prenatally and, if present, a Caesarian section delivery is indicated.
Physical Examination
Usually symmetrically positioned upper and lower extremity contractures
Large and small joints are equally affected.
Facial dysmorphology, other than micrognathia, is uncommon.

Physical Examination
The face may have a characteristic central congenital hemangioma, called a nevus
flammeus, of the forehead, nose, or chin; this finding fades with age (Figure 5). An
underdeveloped mandible is relatively common because of lack of chewing during
pregnancy.

Figure 5 Photograph of the head of an infant with nevus flammeus shows a birthmark
on the forehead. (Courtesy of Shriners Hospital for Children, Philadelphia, PA.)
Scoliosis occurs in approximately 20% to 25% of individuals with arthrogryposis. A small
percentage of babies are born with a curve; because no structural vertebral
abnormalities are present, it is not a congenital scoliosis but a prenatal scoliosis. The
prenatal spine shape reflects the baby’s intrauterine position (Figure 6). Clinical signs of
spinal dysraphism (eg, hairy nevi over the spine) are rare but should be sought.
Extremity contractures usually are symmetric. In the upper extremity, shoulders are
adducted and usually internally rotated, which may impede bringing the hands forward
of the body plane. Elbows most often lack flexion but occasionally have moderate or
severe flexion contractures. Those with flexion contractures more often have severe
hand dysfunction than those with extension contractures. Wrists usually are palmar
flexed, with variable ulnar deviation. Thumbs lack abduction to the point of a thumb-in-
palm deformity. The fingers may lack flexion and extension range and, in patients with
severe involvement, are stiff with a gentle flexion arc and no joint creases.

Hips characteristically have flexion/abduction/external rotation contractures, colloquially
called the Buddha position (Figure 7). This position may be severe enough to obviate
positioning the lower extremities for weight bearing. Approximately 25% of affected hips
are congenitally dislocated. These dislocations occur much earlier in pregnancy and will
be stiffer and higher displaced than idiopathic hip dislocations. Knee flexion contractures
are more common than extension contractures but either can occur. With flexion
contractures, a mild pterygium usually is present behind the knee. In amyoplasia, the
primary foot deformity is the teratologic clubfoot, which is stiffer and more supinated
than the idiopathic clubfoot. A less common foot deformity is a clubfoot variation known
as the equinocavus foot, with a pronounced midfoot cavus but with less heel varus and
adduction.22 Congenital vertical talus is not known to occur with Amyoplasia(Figure 8).

In general, joints appear normal early but show progressive acquired deformity from lack of
motion.
AP pelvis and frog-lateral views help distinguish congenital hip dislocations with contractures
from stable hips with contractures because the clinical appearance of dislocated and reduced
hips with contractures may be identical.
Spine radiographs are not routinely necessary; only used to investigate a clinical deformity.
Ultrasonography
Often not helpful because of technical limitations from hip positioning
Pathology
Amyoplasia is the most common form of AMC but one of the few conditions that appears to be
nongenetic.
The cause of amyoplasia is unknown but theorized to be related to AHC hypoplasia.

Pathology
The cause of amyoplasia is unknown. The leading theory is a vascular insult to the
developing fetus between the eight and eleventh week of gestation.9 That time interval
coincides with the development of the AHCs. AHCs are the cell bodies of the lower motor
neuron; the upper motor neuron synapses with the lower motor neuron in the anterior
horn. A disproportionately large incidence of amyoplasia is associated with monozygotic
twin pregnancies, particularly those with a shared placenta. A possible explanation is
that a mild form of twin-twin transfusion occurs, with the donor twin experiencing a
critical lack of blood flow as the AHCs are developing. Damage to an individual AHC will
inhibit normal development of that particular lower motor neuron, which in turn inhibits
the development of the target muscle.
AHCs maturate in the spinal cord from cephalad to caudad, which may help explain the
varied extremity involvement. A vascular interruption or insult earlier in the critical
period will affect the lower motor nerves of the jaw and upper extremities, whereas later

The CHRNG gene codes for the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) fetal gamma subunit,
disrupting the neurovascular junction during the fetal period.25 This period is critical

gravis, in which autoantibodies to the AChR cross the placenta, disrupting function of the

The treatment goal is to position the hips in the most functional position for walking and

Hip problems can be grouped as flexion contractures, extension contractures, and congenital
hip dislocations.

and tensor fascia lata, just below the anterior superior iliac spine.46 This can be

superior iliac spine. An Ober-like release of the fascia lata just above the level of the

The treatment goal is to straighten the flexed knee appropriately to allow for functional
ambulation and to allow the extended knee to flex to allow for comfortable sitting.
Knee flexion contractures can be classified as mild (<30°), moderate (30° to 50°) or severe

Knee
Knee flexion contractures are more common than extension contractures. Mild
contractures can be managed via femoral anterior-distal hemiepiphysiodesis, slowing
anterior growth of the distal femoral physis while allowing normal posterior growth,
essentially redirecting the distal epiphysis into extension51 Although the articular
femoral-tibial relationship is unchanged, the tibial shaft aligns with the femoral shaft in
full extension (Figure 19). Moderate flexion contractures also can be managed via

releases alone usually do not sufficiently correct a contracture but are a prerequisite for
correction. The direct posterior approach to the popliteal space through the popliteal
fossa necessitates exposure of the neurovascular bundle, which may be anatomically
variable; the approach is even more challenging in patients with pterygia. Instead, a

Knee extension contractures are less common than flexion contractures. They tend not
to hinder ambulation but become problematic in older children when sitting. The
extreme of the hyperextension deformity is a recurvatum deformity, to the point of a
congenital knee dislocation. In babies, initial treatment is serial cast immobilization,
often in combination with cast immobilization of the foot deformity. Because of the lack
of landmarks around the knee and the frequent external rotational contracture of the
hip, accurate determination of the location of the front of the knee is imperative to
prevent an iatrogenic valgus knee deformity by attempting to stretch knee flexion in the
wrong plane. Distal rectus femoris release may be necessary if cast immobilization
fails.55,56 Additional releases may include the medial and lateral patellar retinaculum
and, possibly, anterior capsular release with quadriceps V-Y plasty. In older children, a
Judet quadricepsplasty (elevation of the quadriceps off the femur, with transverse fascial
releases), possibly with femoral shortening, may be indicated.49,57

Feet
Clubfoot deformities are the most common foot findings in patients with AMC and the
only foot deformity in patients with Amyoplasia. In managing arthrogrypotic clubfeet,
surgeons must consider the high rate of relapse during childhood regardless of the
method of correction. Postoperative relapses tend to be stiffer, more painful, and
challenging to correct than in patients with idiopathic clubfeet. Therefore, the emphasis
has shifted to nonsurgical management during childhood. The Ponseti method of
clubfoot cast immobilization is effective in the management of clubfeet in patients with
arthrogryposis.22,58,59 The standard Ponseti stretching and cast immobilization
maneuvers are followed. In patients with severe equinus (>40°), an initial percutaneous
Achilles tenotomy unlocks the calcaneus from the posterior tibia, allowing the calcaneus
to gradually swing out of varus. An AMC clubfoot is stiffer than an idiopathic clubfoot
and usually will require several more casts to achieve correction. An Achilles tenotomy is
almost always necessary after cast immobilization in an infant but is not always required
in patients undergoing cast immobilization for a recurrence. Bracing is crucial after
treatment. The standard Ponseti foot-abduction brace used for the management of
idiopathic clubfoot is not effective because babies with arthrogryposis seldom are
capable of the spontaneous kicking and active ankle motion necessary to stretch their
ankles in the foot-abduction brace. The typical knee flexion and hip flexion/external
rotation contractures also make the foot-abduction brace difficult to fit. An ankle-foot
orthosis molded and padded to correct heel varus and forefoot adduction is essentially
used continuously. At night, detachable medial and lateral dorsiflexion straps are used
to stretch the Achilles tendon. This modified Ponseti method also is effective in older
children with AMC and clubfoot deformities (Figure 21). Typically, children with AMC and
clubfoot deformity have severe external tibial torsion; the residual clubfoot adductus
often compensates for the torsion, but derotational osteotomies occasionally are
required.

Congenital vertical talus is common in patients with distal arthrogryposes and patients
with Escobar syndrome. Management begins with serial cast immobilization via the
reverse Ponseti technique.60,61 Because the forefoot is in an adducted and everted
position, it is gradually stretched into plantar flexion, supination, and adduction. Similar
to Ponseti cast immobilization, the talar head is used as the pivot point, in this case by
placing counter pressure on the palpable talar head in the medial plantar surface of the
foot. The goal is to stretch the lateral ankle and forefoot contracted tissue and attempt
to translate the dislocated navicular from the dorsal neck of the talus to its appropriate
position at the head of the talus (Figure 24). At the completion of cast immobilization,
the talonavicular joint needs to be pinned in the operating room, often via open
reduction of the joint if it did not spontaneously reduce. Postoperative bracing in an
ankle-foot orthosis molded to correct heel valgus and forefoot adductus is necessary.

spastic, forcing the foot into a calcaneus position, which will require adjustments of the
brace to hold the foot plantigrade.

Lower Extremity Treatment Algorithm
Foot deformities are managed during infancy. Clubfoot deformities likely will require
additional cast immobilization during childhood, attempting to limit cast immobilization
sessions to once every year or two.
The hips are managed at an age at which children can begin standing after treatment, usually
after their first birthday.
Open reduction is successful up to and even after 4 years of age; however, earlier open
reduction is preferred.
Hip contractures can be surgically managed at any age but are best managed at a young age
to allow for early ambulation training.
Knee extension contractures can be managed at a young age in many patients, possibly
simultaneously with foot deformity cast immobilization and surgical management or at the
time of hip surgical management.
Knee flexion contractures are best managed after 4 years of age to allow for suitable anatomic
size for the hemiepiphysiodesis plates or external fixator. While waiting for the patient to
reach 4 years of age, the patient should be fitted with knee-ankle-foot orthoses to work on
standing balance and walking.
If possible, procedures requiring general anesthesia should be postponed until after 3 years of
age because of concerns with regard to the effects of anesthesia on the developing brain.
